title: Navigating The Pacific Without Any Instruments
text:
Picture a voyaging canoe several hundred kilometres from any land, carrying no compass, no chart and no instrument of any kind. For a long time European scholars assumed the settlement of the remote Pacific must have been accidental: fishermen blown off course, drifting until they happened to strike an island. That assumption has not survived examination.

Consider the geography first. The islands were settled broadly from west to east, against the prevailing winds, which is the hardest direction in which to drift. The settlers arrived with crops, with pigs and chickens, and in numbers large enough to found lasting populations. That is the cargo of a planned expedition, not of a fishing boat blown out to sea. What made deliberate voyaging possible was a body of navigational knowledge, learned and memorised rather than written down. Navigators held the rising and setting positions of many stars, read swell patterns refracted around unseen land, and watched the flight of seabirds and the colour of clouds above lagoons. Experimental voyages in reconstructed canoes, sailed by navigators trained in surviving traditions, have crossed these distances successfully. The wider point is that technology is not only hardware: a trained memory can do the work we now give to instruments.
points: Scholars once assumed the remote Pacific was settled accidentally by drifting boats.
Settlement ran broadly west to east, against the prevailing winds, which drifting cannot explain.
Voyagers carried crops and domestic animals and arrived in numbers, indicating planned expeditions.
Navigation relied on memorised knowledge rather than written charts or instruments.
Navigators used star positions, swell patterns, seabirds and clouds above lagoons.
Modern voyages in reconstructed canoes have confirmed the methods work over long distances.
